Empirical Research Plan: Bank‐Competition Effects on Small-Firm Credit Supply
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy
   • Method: Two–stage least squares (instrumental variables, “IV-DiD”).  
   • Rationale  
     – The causal object is the effect of local bank-market competition (e.g. deposit-market Herfindahl, HHI) on loan prices/quantities.  
     – Local HHI is endogenous: it is jointly determined with local credit demand, economic conditions, and unobserved bank‐firm matching.  
     – Exogenous variation is provided by state-year legal barriers to out-of-state branch entry created by IBBEA’s opt-out clauses. The Johnson & Rice (2008) 0–4 index captures the “tightness” of those barriers and moved discretely in several states between 1995 and 2003 while others stayed fully open.  
     – Because the index varies across both states and time and is plausibly unrelated to the credit-worthiness of an individual firm surveyed in the SSBF, it is a strong candidate instrument for competition.  
     – We embed the IV in a difference-in-differences framework (state and year fixed effects plus state-specific trends) to net out level differences and common shocks, but the core design is IV.

2. Treatment and Control
   • Endogenous “treatment” variable (second stage):  
     – local_competition_sy = log(HHI) or −HHI in the firm’s home county/MSA in state s, survey year y (lower HHI = more competition).  
   • Instrument (first stage):  
     – restrict_index_sy = 0 … 4 Johnson-Rice branching restriction index for state s in survey year y. Higher values mean tighter barriers → less competition.  
   • Control units: States with index = 0 (fully open) after 1997 as well as all states before IBBEA serve as the counterfactual. All observations enter the 2SLS.  
   • Timing:  
     – “Pre” = 1993 (before interstate branching is legally feasible).  
     – “Post” = 1998 and 2003.  
   • No running variable or cutoff (not an RDD).

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
   A1. Relevance: Branching restrictions materially affect local bank‐market concentration. Bank charter data show large, discrete entry by out-of-state banks in open states only.  
   A2. Exclusion: After controlling for state FE, year FE, state trends, and macro controls, branching restrictions influence small-firm borrowing outcomes solely through their impact on local competition (not via, say, direct credit programs). Because branching statutes apply only to organizational form of banks, this is plausible.  
   A3. Parallel trends / common shocks: Absent changes in branching rules, credit outcomes in high- and low-restriction states would have evolved in parallel. Including state-specific linear trends and lagged state income growth helps.  
   A4. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): A firm’s borrowing outcomes are affected only by its own state’s branching rules, not by those of other states (reasonable for small firms with local banking relationships).  
   A5. Monotonicity (IV): Lower legal barriers never reduce competition for any local market (no “defiers”). Theory and historic entry patterns support this.

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
   1. Political endogeneity of restrictions: States with fragile small-business sectors may have lobbied for tighter rules, biasing results.  
      – Mitigation: (i) Add state × pre-trend controls (five-year lagged small-business share, per-capita income growth), (ii) include state fixed effects and state-specific linear trends, (iii) placebo test on 1987–1992 Business Census data to show no pre-policy differential trends.  
   2. Omitted local demand shocks: Downturns could simultaneously raise loan rates and change deposit HHIs.  
      – Mitigation: Control for county unemployment, state GDP growth, industry mix; cluster SEs at state level; include MSA-year fixed effects in robustness.  
   3. Sample-selection in SSBF (only ~40 % report a recent loan): If competition also affects the likelihood of having a loan, 2SLS on the selected sample may be biased.  
      – Mitigation: Estimate a Heckman selection model with the extensive margin (has_loan) in the first stage; show that IV results are robust to inverse Mills correction; replicate using the full sample with imputed interest rate = NA and use a tobit-IV for loan amount.

5. R Code Outline (simplified)

```r
# Install/load packages
packages <- c("data.table","fixest","readr","haven","stringr","dplyr","sandwich","lmtest")
lapply(packages, require, character.only=TRUE)

# 1. Data loading ----------------------------------------------------------
ssbf93 <- fread("SSBF_1993.csv")
ssbf98 <- fread("SSBF_1998.csv")
ssbf03 <- fread("SSBF_2003.csv")
restrict <- fread("state_restrict_index.csv")   # state, year, restrict_index
hhi      <- fread("msa_hhi.csv")                # msa, year, hhi
macro    <- fread("macro_controls.csv")         # year, prime, term_spread, default_spread
stateeco <- fread("state_controls.csv")         # state, year, pc_income_growth, unemployment

# Stack SSBF files
ssbf <- rbindlist(list(ssbf93, ssbf98, ssbf03), use.names=TRUE, fill=TRUE)

# 2. Merge instruments and controls ----------------------------------------
ssbf <- ssbf %>% 
        mutate(year = survey_year,
               state = state_fips,
               msa   = msa_code) %>%
        left_join(restrict,  by = c("state","year")) %>%
        left_join(hhi,       by = c("msa","year")) %>%
        left_join(macro,     by = "year")          %>%
        left_join(stateeco,  by = c("state","year"))

# 3. Variable construction -------------------------------------------------
ssbf <- ssbf %>%
        mutate(log_hhi    = log(hhi),
               competition = -log_hhi,            # higher = more competition
               int_rate    = loan_interest_rate,  # outcome 1
               ln_loan_amt = log(loan_amount) )   # outcome 2

# 4. First–stage & second–stage -------------------------------------------
# 2SLS with state & year FE, state trends
iv_formula <- int_rate ~ competition + prime + term_spread + default_spread |
                          restrict_index + prime + term_spread + default_spread

mod_2sls  <- feols(iv_formula,
                   data = ssbf,
                   fixef = ~ state + year + state[year],   # state trends
                   cluster = ~ state)

summary(mod_2sls)

# 5. Robustness: placebo using pre-IBBEA subsample (1988 Census) ----------
# (assuming we loaded a pre-period dataset ‘census88’ with small-firm borrowing vars)
# Estimate same model on 1988 data – restrict_index set to future values – expect β ≈ 0.

# 6. Robustness: alternative competition measure --------------------------
ssbf <- ssbf %>% mutate(num_banks = 1/hhi)   # simple alternative
mod_alt <- feols(int_rate ~ num_banks | restrict_index, 
                 data = ssbf,
                 fixef = ~ state + year + state[year],
                 cluster = ~ state)
summary(mod_alt)
```

6. Expected Results
   • Theory (Petersen–Rajan 1995; Cetorelli-Strahan 2006) predicts that more competition lowers lending rates but may only modestly expand quantities if asymmetric-information frictions remain.  
   • A 1-SD decrease in HHI (~0.5 log-points) should reduce small-firm loan rates by roughly 40–70 basis points (≈ 7 % of the sample mean 9 % rate) and raise loan size by 6–10 %.  
   • Collateral requirements may fall slightly; maturity likely shortens as banks compete on price rather than covenant length.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV Method)
   C1: Strong first-stage (F-stat > 10)...................... 1  
   C2: Exclusion restriction plausible....................... 0.5  
   C3: No differential pre-trends (parallel trends).......... 0.5  
   C4: Correct standard-error clustering..................... 1  
   C5: Robustness to alternative specifications.............. 1  
   Total (out of 5).......................................... 4  

Overall, the IV-DiD design using state branching barriers provides credible causal estimates of how heightened bank competition transmits to small-firm borrowing costs and quantities, subject to careful checks on political endogeneity and sample selection.
